Here is what we are figuring out: a taxi fare follows a rule with a letter x in it, and x is how far the ride is. Our rule is three x plus two, and the ride is four km. We drop the four in for x, so three x becomes three times four, then we work it out in order — times before plus.
Welcome to the taxi meter. The fare follows a rule with a letter x in it — x is how far the ride is. This rule is three x plus two, and this ride is four km.
First we drop the four in wherever we see x. So three x becomes three times four. Now it is just numbers: three times four plus two.
Now work it out in order — times before plus. Tap the times: three times four is twelve.
Only the plus is left. Twelve plus two.
Tap it — twelve plus two is fourteen. One number is left, so the fare is fourteen dollars.
When the fare is worked out, set it. Now let's try one together.
Your turn — I will help. The fare rule is x plus two. Drop in three for x, then tap the plus.
The fare rule is 2x + 1, where x is the km. Drop in 3 for x, then work it out — times before plus.
Put 3 in place of x: 2 × 3 + 1.
It was 7.
The meter charges 3 dollars a km, then 2 dollars a km on top. What does one km cost altogether?
Combine like terms — add the counts of x.
It was 5x.
The fare rule is 2(x + 3), where x is the km. Drop in 4 for x, then work it out — times before plus.
Put 4 in place of x: 2 × (4 + 3).
It was 14.
The fare rule is 3x, where x is the km. Drop in 3 for x, then work it out — times before plus.
Put 3 in place of x: 3 × 3.
It was 9.
The fare rule is x + 5, where x is the km. Drop in 4 for x, then work it out — times before plus.
Put 4 in place of x: 4 + 5.
The fare came to 10 dollars using the rule 3x − 2. How many km was the ride?
Which x makes 3x − 2 equal 10?
It was 4.
The fare came to 12 dollars using the rule x + 7. How many km was the ride?
Which x makes x + 7 equal 12?
It was 5.
The meter charges 4 dollars a km, then 3 dollars a km on top. What does one km cost altogether?
It was 7x.
The fare came to 20 dollars using the rule 4x. How many km was the ride?
Which x makes 4x equal 20?
The fare rule is 4x − 3, where x is the km. Drop in 5 for x, then work it out — times before plus.
Put 5 in place of x: 4 × 5 − 3.
It was 17.
The meter charges 5 dollars a km, then takes 2 dollars a km back off. What does one km cost altogether?
It was 3x.
The fare came to 11 dollars using the rule 2x + 1. How many km was the ride?
Which x makes 2x + 1 equal 11?
The meter charges 6 dollars a km, then takes 2 dollars a km back off. What does one km cost altogether?
It was 4x.

Here is what we are figuring out: every drop-off on the map is two numbers — an across number and an up-or-down number. We will fly the drone to three, minus two: three across, then two down, so you can read a coordinate and land right on it.
Delivery drone! This is the city map. Every drop-off has two numbers — an across number and an up-or-down number.
The two numbers are called x and y. The first one, x, is the ACROSS. The second one, y, is UP or DOWN.
Always start at the middle — zero, zero. That's the drone base, right in the centre.
Our drop-off is three, minus two. Let's read it one number at a time.
First number is three — that's the across, x. A positive number means go RIGHT.
So count one, to the right.
Two, keep going right.
Three. Now we're three across, sitting on the middle line.
Second number is minus two — that's the up-or-down, y. A negative number means go DOWN.
So count one, down below the line.
Two, keep going down.
We've landed on three, minus two — three across, two down. That's the drop-off!
Drop the package right there. When you're on the drop-off, press drop. Now let's try one together.
Your turn — I will help. Deliver to two, one. Fly two across, then one up, then press drop.
Fly the drone to 3, 2. Tap the map.
Fly 3 across first (x), then 2 up or down (y).
That drops it at (3, 2).
It was (3, 2).
The drone is at -2, 1. Move it 3 left and 1 up, then tap where it lands.
Across: −2 − 3 = −5. Up/down: 1 + 1 = 2.
It was (-5, 2).
Fly the drone to the halfway point between -2, 0 and 2, 4.
Halfway across: (−2 + 2) ÷ 2 = 0.
Halfway up/down: (0 + 4) ÷ 2 = 2. So (0, 2).
It was (0, 2).
Fly the drone to 1, 3. Tap the map.
Fly 1 across first (x), then 3 up or down (y).
That drops it at (1, 3).
It was (1, 3).
The drone is at -2, 1. Move it 3 right and 2 down, then tap where it lands.
Across: −2 + 3 = 1. Up/down: 1 − 2 = −1.
It was (1, -1).
Reflect the drop-off -2, 4 across the x-axis, then deliver it.
Flipping up ↔ down keeps the across number and flips the sign of the up/down number.
Fly the drone to 5, -3. Tap the map.
Fly 5 across first (x), then −3 up or down (y).
That drops it at (5, −3).
It was (5, -3).
Fly the drone to 2, 4. Tap the map.
Fly 2 across first (x), then 4 up or down (y).
That drops it at (2, 4).
It was (2, 4).
Fly the drone to 2, -4. Tap the map.
Fly 2 across first (x), then −4 up or down (y).
That drops it at (2, −4).
It was (2, -4).
The drone is at 2, -1. Move it 3 left and 1 up, then tap where it lands.
Across: 2 − 3 = −1. Up/down: −1 + 1 = 0.
It was (-1, 0).
Reflect the drop-off 3, -1 across the y-axis, then deliver it.
Flipping left ↔ right keeps the up/down number and flips the sign of the across number.
The drone is at -2, 1. Move it 2 right and 3 up, then tap where it lands.
Across: −2 + 2 = 0. Up/down: 1 + 3 = 4.
It was (0, 4).
Reflect the drop-off -2, 4 across the y-axis, then deliver it.
The drone is at -1, -2. Move it 2 right and 3 up, then tap where it lands.
Across: −1 + 2 = 1. Up/down: −2 + 3 = 1.
It was (1, 1).
Fly the drone to the halfway point between 2, 2 and 4, 6.
Halfway across: (2 + 4) ÷ 2 = 3.
Halfway up/down: (2 + 6) ÷ 2 = 4. So (3, 4).
It was (3, 4).
Fly the drone to 5, 2. Tap the map.
Fly 5 across first (x), then 2 up or down (y).
That drops it at (5, 2).
It was (5, 2).
The drone is at -2, 1. Move it 2 left and 2 down, then tap where it lands.
Across: −2 − 2 = −4. Up/down: 1 − 2 = −1.
Fly the drone to -4, 2. Tap the map.
Fly −4 across first (x), then 2 up or down (y).
That drops it at (−4, 2).
It was (-4, 2).
The drone is at 2, -1. Move it 2 left and 2 down, then tap where it lands.
Across: 2 − 2 = 0. Up/down: −1 − 2 = −3.
It was (0, -3).
Reflect the drop-off 3, 2 across the x-axis, then deliver it.
It was (3, -2).
Fly the drone to 4, 1. Tap the map.
Fly 4 across first (x), then 1 up or down (y).
That drops it at (4, 1).
It was (4, 1).
Fly the drone to -3, -2. Tap the map.
Fly −3 across first (x), then −2 up or down (y).
That drops it at (−3, −2).
The drone is at 1, 1. Move it 1 right and 3 down, then tap where it lands.
Across: 1 + 1 = 2. Up/down: 1 − 3 = −2.
It was (2, -2).
Fly the drone to -2, -3. Tap the map.
Fly −2 across first (x), then −3 up or down (y).
That drops it at (−2, −3).
The drone is at 2, -1. Move it 3 right and 2 down, then tap where it lands.
Across: 2 + 3 = 5. Up/down: −1 − 2 = −3.
The drone is at 2, 2. Move it 3 right and 2 down, then tap where it lands.
Across: 2 + 3 = 5. Up/down: 2 − 2 = 0.
It was (5, 0).
The drone is at 2, 2. Move it 2 left and 2 down, then tap where it lands.
Across: 2 − 2 = 0. Up/down: 2 − 2 = 0.
It was (0, 0).
The drone is at -1, -2. Move it 1 right and 3 down, then tap where it lands.
Across: −1 + 1 = 0. Up/down: −2 − 3 = −5.
It was (0, -5).
The drone is at 1, 1. Move it 2 left and 2 down, then tap where it lands.
Across: 1 − 2 = −1. Up/down: 1 − 2 = −1.
The drone is at -1, -2. Move it 2 left and 2 down, then tap where it lands.
The drone is at 2, 2. Move it 2 right and 3 up, then tap where it lands.
Across: 2 + 2 = 4. Up/down: 2 + 3 = 5.
It was (4, 5).
The drone is at 2, 2. Move it 1 right and 3 down, then tap where it lands.
Across: 2 + 1 = 3. Up/down: 2 − 3 = −1.
It was (3, -1).
The drone is at 1, 1. Move it 3 left and 1 up, then tap where it lands.
Across: 1 − 3 = −2. Up/down: 1 + 1 = 2.
It was (-2, 2).
The drone is at -2, 1. Move it 1 right and 3 down, then tap where it lands.
Across: −2 + 1 = −1. Up/down: 1 − 3 = −2.
The drone is at 1, 1. Move it 3 right and 2 down, then tap where it lands.
Across: 1 + 3 = 4. Up/down: 1 − 2 = −1.
It was (4, -1).
The drone is at 1, 1. Move it 2 right and 3 up, then tap where it lands.
Across: 1 + 2 = 3. Up/down: 1 + 3 = 4.
The drone is at -1, -2. Move it 3 left and 1 up, then tap where it lands.
The drone is at 2, -1. Move it 1 right and 3 down, then tap where it lands.
Across: 2 + 1 = 3. Up/down: −1 − 3 = −4.
It was (3, -4).
The drone is at 2, -1. Move it 2 right and 3 up, then tap where it lands.
Across: 2 + 2 = 4. Up/down: −1 + 3 = 2.
It was (4, 2).
The drone is at -1, -2. Move it 3 right and 2 down, then tap where it lands.
Across: −1 + 3 = 2. Up/down: −2 − 2 = −4.
The drone is at 2, 2. Move it 3 left and 1 up, then tap where it lands.
Across: 2 − 3 = −1. Up/down: 2 + 1 = 3.
It was (-1, 3).

Here is what we are figuring out: a check-in scale balances only when both pans weigh the same. The left pan holds a mystery case plus a three-kilo weight, and the right pan reads eight kilos. We will find the case's weight — the x that makes x plus three equal eight — and it comes out to five.
Airport check-in scale! For the scale to sit level, both pans must weigh exactly the same.
The left pan holds the mystery case plus a three-kilo weight. The right pan reads eight kilos.
So we need the left pan — the case plus three — to match eight. Let's find the case's weight one kilo at a time.
Right now x is zero — an empty case. The left is only three kilos, so it's too light. The scale tips down on the right.
Let's make the case heavier. x equals one: the left pan is one plus three, that's four kilos. Still too light.
x equals two: the left pan grows to two plus three, five kilos. Getting closer, but still under eight.
x equals three: three plus three is six kilos. The scale is levelling out but not there yet.
x equals four: four plus three is seven kilos. Almost balanced — just one kilo short.
x equals five: five plus three is eight kilos. Now both pans read eight — the scale is balanced!
Another way to see it: take three kilos off both pans and the case alone equals five. Same answer.
Balanced means solved: the mystery case weighs five kilos. Press weigh when it's level. Next, a different kind of rule.
Now a different kind of rule. Sometimes a case doesn't need an exact weight — it just has a LIMIT. This case plus its two-kilo tag must weigh at most six kilos.
Solve it just like an equation. Take two off both sides: x is at most four.
But four isn't the only answer. Three works, two works, even zero works — every weight four or under is allowed.
So we shade the whole line from four downward. That shaded ray is every weight the case is allowed to be.
The dot on four is FILLED IN, because four itself is allowed. 'At most four' includes four.
If the rule said UNDER four instead — less than four — the dot would be HOLLOW, because four would no longer count.
Ours is 'at most', so keep it filled. Pick the symbol, set the edge, then set the rule. Now let's try one together.
Your turn — I will help. The case balances when x plus one equals four. Work out x. What does the case weigh?
One more — a weight rule this time. This case has a rule: x plus 2 is at most 6. Work out x, then pick the symbol and set the edge weight.
The case balances when 2x equals 10 kilograms. Work out x. What does the case weigh, in kilograms?
Find the x that makes 2x equal 10.
x = 5 makes both pans read 10.
It was x = 5.
Solve: x plus 1 is under 5. Work out x, then pick the symbol and set the edge weight.
Solve for x: x + 1 < 5 means x < 4.
4 is NOT allowed, so the dot is hollow. Shade every weight under 4.
It was x < 4.
The case balances when x divided by 2 equals 6 kilograms. Work out x. What does the case weigh, in kilograms?
Find the x that makes x ÷ 2 equal 6.
x = 12 makes both pans read 6.
It was x = 12.
The case balances when x plus 3 equals 7 kilograms. Work out x. What does the case weigh, in kilograms?
Find the x that makes x + 3 equal 7.
x = 4 makes both pans read 7.
It was x = 4.
The case balances when 2x plus 5 equals 17 kilograms. Work out x. What does the case weigh, in kilograms?
Find the x that makes 2x + 5 equal 17.
x = 6 makes both pans read 17.
It was x = 6.
The case balances when 5x equals 15 kilograms. Work out x. What does the case weigh, in kilograms?
Find the x that makes 5x equal 15.
x = 3 makes both pans read 15.
It was x = 3.
The case balances when 4x minus 1 equals 11 kilograms. Work out x. What does the case weigh, in kilograms?
Find the x that makes 4x − 1 equal 11.
x = 3 makes both pans read 11.
The case balances when 3x equals 12 kilograms. Work out x. What does the case weigh, in kilograms?
Find the x that makes 3x equal 12.
x = 4 makes both pans read 12.
Solve: 2x is over 6. Work out x, then pick the symbol and set the edge weight.
Solve for x: 2x > 6 means x > 3.
3 is NOT allowed, so the dot is hollow. Shade every weight over 3.
It was x > 3.
Solve: 3x is over 12. Work out x, then pick the symbol and set the edge weight.
Solve for x: 3x > 12 means x > 4.
4 is NOT allowed, so the dot is hollow. Shade every weight over 4.
It was x > 4.
Solve: 2x is at least 6. Work out x, then pick the symbol and set the edge weight.
Solve for x: 2x ≥ 6 means x ≥ 3.
3 itself is allowed, so the dot is filled. Shade every weight at least 3.
It was x ≥ 3.
Solve: x plus 5 is under 8. Work out x, then pick the symbol and set the edge weight.
Solve for x: x + 5 < 8 means x < 3.
3 is NOT allowed, so the dot is hollow. Shade every weight under 3.
It was x < 3.
The case balances when 3x minus 2 equals 10 kilograms. Work out x. What does the case weigh, in kilograms?
Find the x that makes 3x − 2 equal 10.
x = 4 makes both pans read 10.
Solve: 2x plus 1 is at most 9. Work out x, then pick the symbol and set the edge weight.
Solve for x: 2x + 1 ≤ 9 means x ≤ 4.
4 itself is allowed, so the dot is filled. Shade every weight at most 4.
It was x ≤ 4.
The case balances when x minus 4 equals 1 kilograms. Work out x. What does the case weigh, in kilograms?
Find the x that makes x − 4 equal 1.
x = 5 makes both pans read 1.
The case balances when 2x plus 3 equals 11 kilograms. Work out x. What does the case weigh, in kilograms?
Find the x that makes 2x + 3 equal 11.
x = 4 makes both pans read 11.
Solve: x minus 1 is at least 3. Work out x, then pick the symbol and set the edge weight.
Solve for x: x − 1 ≥ 3 means x ≥ 4.
4 itself is allowed, so the dot is filled. Shade every weight at least 4.
It was x ≥ 4.
Solve: x plus 2 is at most 6. Work out x, then pick the symbol and set the edge weight.
Solve for x: x + 2 ≤ 6 means x ≤ 4.

Welcome to the Tile Factory! Today's order is three squared — that little two means squared.
Three squared means three multiplied by itself — three times three.
Every build starts at one, before we lay any tiles. Watch the counter.
One turn of the crank multiplies by three. So turn once.
One times three is three — that is our first row of three tiles.
Now turn again to lay another row. That multiplies by three once more.
Three times three is nine tiles.
We've turned twice — that's three multiplied twice. That's what squared means.
So three squared is nine. Nine tiles fill the patch.
Laid one layer too many? Just turn the handle back the other way to undo it.

Here is what we are figuring out: we are tiling a room floor, and to find the area we don't calculate — we lay tiles and count them. The floor is six metres long and four wide, so we lay four rows of six tiles and the tiles that cover it are the area.
Time to renovate! First job: tile a floor. To find the AREA, we don't calculate — we lay tiles and count them. This floor is six metres long and four wide.
Lay the first row — six tiles fit along the length.
Lay the second row — that's twelve tiles so far.
Third row — eighteen.
The last row fills the floor — twenty-four tiles. That's four rows of six.
The tiles cover twenty-four square metres — that IS the area. When it's covered, order them. Now let's try one together.
Your turn — I will help. This floor is three by two metres. Lay tiles across the whole floor. The tiles you place are the area.
This room is 5 by 3 metres. The perimeter is the whole distance around its edge — all four sides added up.
Perimeter = the edge all the way round = 2 × (width + height).
A round pond is 2 metres from the middle to the edge. Work out two times 2 — that is how many pi the distance round it is.
The distance round a circle = 2 × π × radius.
2 × 2 = 4, so it is 4π.
It was 4π.
This roof is half of a 4 by 3 metre rectangle. Work out the whole rectangle first, then halve it.
The whole rectangle: 4 × 3 = 12 m².
The triangle is half of it: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 m².
This room is 4 by 3 metres. The perimeter is the whole distance around its edge — all four sides added up.
A round pond is 4 metres from the middle to the edge. Work out two times 4 — that is how many pi the distance round it is.
2 × 4 = 8, so it is 8π.
It was 8π.
A brace cuts across a square corner, 3 metres along one wall and 4 up the other. Square each wall length, add them, then find what number times itself gives that.
Square each wall side and add: 3 × 3 + 4 × 4 = 25.
The brace times itself must give 25, so the brace is 5 m.
This floor is 4 by 3 metres. Its area is how many one-metre tiles cover it.
Floor area = the tiles that cover it = length × width.
A round patio is 4 metres from the middle to the edge. Work out 4 squared — that is how many pi the area is.
A circle’s area = π × radius × radius.
4 × 4 = 16, so the area is 16π.
It was 16π.
A square corner has a sloping side of 10 metres and one wall of 6. Square the sloping side, take away the square of the wall you know, then find what number times itself gives what is left.
Square the sloping side, take away the known wall squared: 10 × 10 − 6 × 6 = 64.
The missing wall times itself must give 64, so it is 8 m.
This floor is 5 by 2 metres. Its area is how many one-metre tiles cover it.
This roof is half of a 5 by 4 metre rectangle. Work out the whole rectangle first, then halve it.
The whole rectangle: 5 × 4 = 20 m².
The triangle is half of it: 20 ÷ 2 = 10 m².
A round pond is 6 metres from the middle to the edge. Work out two times 6 — that is how many pi the distance round it is.
2 × 6 = 12, so it is 12π.
It was 12π.
A square corner has a sloping side of 5 metres and one wall of 4. Square the sloping side, take away the square of the wall you know, then find what number times itself gives what is left.
Square the sloping side, take away the known wall squared: 5 × 5 − 4 × 4 = 9.
The missing wall times itself must give 9, so it is 3 m.

The whole rectangle: 3 × 4 = 12 m².

A round patio is 5 metres from the middle to the edge. Work out 5 squared — that is how many pi the area is.

A brace cuts across a square corner, 6 metres along one wall and 8 up the other. Square each wall length, add them, then find what number times itself gives that.
Square each wall side and add: 6 × 6 + 8 × 8 = 100.
The brace times itself must give 100, so the brace is 10 m.
A square corner has a sloping side of 13 metres and one wall of 5. Square the sloping side, take away the square of the wall you know, then find what number times itself gives what is left.
Square the sloping side, take away the known wall squared: 13 × 13 − 5 × 5 = 144.
The missing wall times itself must give 144, so it is 12 m.
This roof is half of a 8 by 3 metre rectangle. Work out the whole rectangle first, then halve it.
The whole rectangle: 8 × 3 = 24 m².
A round pond is 5 metres from the middle to the edge. Work out two times 5 — that is how many pi the distance round it is.
2 × 5 = 10, so it is 10π.
It was 10π.

2 × 2 = 4, so the area is 4π.

Here is what we are figuring out: a bank balance can go below zero when you spend more than you have. We will start at four dollars, take away seven, and land in overdraft — that is subtracting to get a negative number.
This is your account meter. Zero is the middle line. Above zero is money you have, below zero is overdraft. Let us work one out together, nice and slow.
Our question: the balance starts at four dollars, then you withdraw seven. Let us build it up one step at a time.
First, the starting balance. Four dollars, up here above zero.
Withdraw means money goes OUT, so we count DOWN. Take away seven, one dollar at a time.
Take one dollar: four goes down to three.
Take another: three goes down to two.
Again: two goes down to one.
And one more brings us all the way down to zero. That is four dollars gone — the account is empty.
But we had to take away SEVEN, and we have only taken four. Three more to go — so now we drop BELOW zero, into overdraft.
Take the fifth dollar: zero goes down to minus one. We are now in the red.
The sixth dollar: minus one goes down to minus two.
The seventh and last dollar: minus two goes down to minus three.
We took away all seven. It landed on minus three — three dollars in overdraft. So four minus seven is minus three.

Here is what we are figuring out: a water tank fills at a steady rate, so its level makes a straight line over time. We will track a tank that starts at one litre and fills two litres every minute, and write that as y = 2x + 1 — the start plus the rate times the minutes.
Tank duty! The water level depends on two things: where it STARTS, and how fast it FILLS. Let us find them one at a time.
The pattern we want is y = 2x + 1. The number on its OWN is the start. The number stuck to x is the fill rate.
First the start level — the number on its own. Here it is one, so the tank begins at one litre.
So I lift the start to one litre. Watch the whole line rise up to begin at one.
Now the fill RATE — the number with x. Here it is two, so the level rises two litres every single minute.
I set the rate dial to two litres a minute. Now the line tilts up two for every step across.
Let us check it. Start at one. After one minute add two: one plus two is three litres.
After two minutes add two more: one plus four is five litres. Every point sits right on the line.
That straight line IS the tank filling — start at one, up two each minute.
Start level first, then fill rate. Press set line when it fits. Now let's try one together.
Your turn — I will help. Set the start level to one litre, then a fill rate of one — up one litre every minute. Then press set line.
The tank starts EMPTY. After 1 min it reads 1 litres. How many litres does it fill each minute?
No starting water, so it is just rate × time — y = mx.
Rate = 1 ÷ 1 = 1 litres a minute; start 0.
It was 1 litres a minute.
Match the tank's fill: it reads (0, 3) and (1, 4). Set the start level and fill rate so the water level over time hits both readings.
Fill rate = change in level ÷ change in time between the readings.
Fills 1 litres a minute, starting at 3.
It was fill rate 1, start 3.
This tank is DRAINING. It reads (0, 4) then (1, 2). Set the start level and the fill rate — the rate is negative — so the line hits both.
Draining means the rate is NEGATIVE.
It was fill rate -2, start 4.
Match the tank's fill: it reads (0, 2) and (1, 3). Set the start level and fill rate so the water level over time hits both readings.
Fills 1 litres a minute, starting at 2.
It was fill rate 1, start 2.
The sensor drew the tank's fill as this line. Which rule matches it?
Read the line's height at minute 0 — where it crosses the up-and-down middle line. That is the START (b = 2).
It climbs -1 for each step right — the RATE. So y = −x + 2.
It was y = −x + 2.
The tank starts EMPTY. After 1 min it reads 2 litres. How many litres does it fill each minute?
Rate = 2 ÷ 1 = 2 litres a minute; start 0.
It was 2 litres a minute.
Match the tank's fill: it reads (0, 1) and (1, 3). Set the start level and fill rate so the water level over time hits both readings.
Fills 2 litres a minute, starting at 1.
It was fill rate 2, start 1.
The tank starts EMPTY. After 2 min it reads 6 litres. How many litres does it fill each minute?
Rate = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 litres a minute; start 0.
It was 3 litres a minute.
The tank fills 2 litres a minute. After 2 min it reads 5 litres. How many litres did it START with?
The rate is given: 2 litres a minute.
Start = level − rate × time = 5 − 2×2 = 1.
It was starts at 1 litres.
A sensor logged the tank over time. Is it a STEADY tank — exactly one level at each minute?
One minute shows TWO different levels — a steady tank cannot do that.
A time with two outputs is NOT a function.
It was no — a minute had two levels.
Read the line's height at minute 0 — where it crosses the up-and-down middle line. That is the START (b = 0).
It climbs 3 for each step right — the RATE. So y = 3x.
It was y = 3x.
Match the tank's fill: it reads (0, 1) and (2, 5). Set the start level and fill rate so the water level over time hits both readings.
The tank fills 3 litres a minute. After 1 min it reads 4 litres. How many litres did it START with?
The rate is given: 3 litres a minute.
Start = level − rate × time = 4 − 3×1 = 1.
Every minute has exactly ONE level — that is a function.
One input, one output: a steady tank.
It was yes — one level each minute.
Read the line's height at minute 0 — where it crosses the up-and-down middle line. That is the START (b = 1).
It climbs 2 for each step right — the RATE. So y = 2x + 1.
It was y = 2x + 1.

Welcome to the checkout. First, what does a percent actually mean? This grid has one hundred little squares.
Percent means "out of a hundred". So twenty-five percent is twenty-five of the hundred squares.
Watch twenty-five squares shade in. See how it fills one corner — a quarter of the whole grid.
So twenty-five percent is the same as one quarter. Hold on to that.
Now a real order: a hoodie, eighty dollars, twenty-five percent off. This slider is the price.
We just saw twenty-five percent is a quarter. A quarter of eighty dollars is twenty dollars.
So take twenty dollars off. Slide the price down — seventy…
…and down to sixty dollars. Eighty take away twenty is sixty.
Sixty dollars is the sale price. Press ring it up when it's right. Now let's try one together.

Here is what we are figuring out: taking a part of a part. Our board is two-thirds of a metre, and we need half of that — so we will work out half of two-thirds by marking a board split into twelve equal parts.
Welcome to the cutting bench. This board is split into twelve equal parts. Tapping a part marks it.
Our job says: the board is two-thirds of a metre, and we need half of that. Let us build it up slowly.
First, what is two-thirds of the board? Split the twelve parts into three equal groups. Twelve shared into three groups is four parts in each group.
One third is one of those groups — four parts. Watch four parts light up.
Two thirds is two groups. Four parts, and four more, makes eight parts.
So the board for this cut is these eight parts. Now we take HALF of the eight.
Half means split the eight into two equal groups. Half of eight is four. Watch four marks switch off.
Four parts stay marked. Four out of twelve parts is four-twelfths.
And four-twelfths is the same as one-third of a metre. That is our first cut.
Now the tape measure. It slides from zero to one metre. Let us work out zero-point-five times zero-point-four.
Zero-point-four means four-tenths of a metre. Slide the tape out to zero-point-four.
Zero-point-five means one half. So we want half of that zero-point-four.
Half of zero-point-four is zero-point-two. Slide the tape back to zero-point-two.
So zero-point-five times zero-point-four is zero-point-two. See how multiplying by less than one makes it smaller.
Last one — dividing by a fraction. How many quarter-metre pieces can we cut from three-quarters of a board?
Here is the trick: three-quarters is really three quarter-pieces stuck together.
So count the quarter-pieces: one, two, three. Slide across to three.
Three-quarters divided by one-quarter is three. Dividing asks how many fit — and three pieces fit.
When your cut is set, press Cut. Now let's try one together.

This is your money meter — your net worth. Above the zero line you have money, in the green. Drop below zero and you are in the red — in debt. Let us work out two minus five.
You start with two dollars, so your worth is up in the green.
Minus five means you pay out five dollars. Paying takes your worth DOWN. Watch it drop, one dollar at a time.
Pay one — down to one dollar.
Pay another — down to zero. You are broke, right on the line.
Pay a third — now you drop below zero. You OWE a dollar: minus one.
Pay a fourth — you owe two.
Pay the fifth — you owe three dollars. Your worth is minus three.
Times works differently — instead of sliding the meter, we lay out cards. A coin is money, a red IOU is debt. Let us do negative five times negative two.
The second number, negative two, tells us what each card is: a two-dollar DEBT. A red IOU.
How many? Five cards. So here are five two-dollar IOUs.
Now the FIRST number, negative five, is the action. Negative means TAKE THEM AWAY. Watch what happens to your worth when the debts leave.
The five IOUs are gone — that is ten dollars of debt you no longer owe. Your worth climbs all the way up to positive ten.
So negative five times negative two is positive ten. Take away debt, and you get richer — that is why two negatives make a positive.
Divide asks a different question: how do we REACH a worth. We want a worth of negative eighteen — that means we owe eighteen dollars.
Each card is a six-dollar IOU. To OWE money, we ADD debt. Add one IOU — now we owe six.
Add another — we owe twelve.
Add a third — now we owe eighteen. That hits the target exactly. It took three cards, and we ADDED them.
We added three, so the answer is positive three. Negative eighteen divided by negative six is positive three.

Here's a power-up: two to the fourth. Let's charge it up together, nice and slow.
That little four is the exponent. It says two is used as a factor four times.
Every stat starts at one, at level zero — before any power-up. That is why anything to the power zero is one.
Crank up one level. One times two is two. The meter leaps.
Crank again, level two. Two times two is four — it doubled once more.
Level three. Four times two is eight — doubling gets big fast.
Level four, the last one. Eight times two is sixteen. The meter is full.
Look at what we did — we started at one and multiplied by two once per level, four levels over.
So two to the fourth is sixteen. The exponent counted the levels, and the level counter agrees: four.
Now a harder one. Two power-ups, both base two: two cubed, and two squared. We fit one on top of the other.
Start at one again, level zero, and crank the first one out. Three levels: two, four, eight.
The level counter reads three. That is the three in two cubed — it has been counting our turns all along.
Now stack the second power-up on top. Two squared is two more levels — do not start over, just keep cranking.
And the second of them. The stat is thirty-two.
Watch the counter: it went to three, then two more, and stopped at five. Three plus two is five.
That is the whole rule. Same base, stacked, and the levels ADD. Two cubed times two squared is two to the fifth: thirty-two.
Last one. A debuff — it does the opposite of a power-up. Every level it drags you down, it divides your stat by two.
Turning the crank backwards is how we divide. Here we are at level zero, stat one.
Turn it back once. One divided by two is one half. The counter drops below zero, to negative one.
Turn it back again. One half divided by two is one quarter, at level negative two.
So the minus sign in the exponent is not a minus on the answer — the stat never goes below nothing. It is a direction: back down the levels.
Two to the negative two is one quarter — which is one over two squared. Below zero, the level turns into the bottom of a fraction.
Build the power-up 2 to the 4. Crank it up 4 levels — each turn multiplies your stat by 2.
2⁴ means 2 used as a factor 4 times — start at 1 and multiply by 2 once per level: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.
3 to the 2, all raised to the 2. That is a batch of 2 levels, run 2 times over. Crank it out and read the stat.

Here is the plan. A ticket price can be written as one expression with a letter in it, like three x plus five, where x is how many tickets. To get the total, we put the number of tickets in place of x and work it out. Let us do one together, nice and slow.
Here's a ticket order. The price is written as an expression: three x plus five.
That letter x isn't a mystery — it just stands for the number of tickets you buy.
Today you're buying two tickets. So for this order, x is two.
The three in front of the x is the price of one ticket: three dollars each.
The plus five is a booking fee — added once, no matter how many tickets.
To find the total, we swap the x for its value. Put two where the x was: three times two, plus five.
Work out the ticket part first: three times two is six. Six dollars of tickets.
Now the order reads six plus five.
Add the five-dollar booking fee on top.
Six plus five is eleven.
So the whole order comes to eleven dollars. Eleven is the total.
Same shop, a messier price. This one was written out in four pieces, and we want it tidy.
Two of the pieces carry an x. Two x and four x — those are ticket pieces, priced per ticket.
The other two are plain numbers. Three and one — those are fees, paid once.
Only pieces of the same kind can join. Ticket pieces join ticket pieces, fees join fees.
Join the ticket pieces first. Two x and four x make six x.
So the per-ticket slot is six. Set it to six.
Now the fees. Three and one make four.
Set the fee slot to four. Six x plus four — the same price, written tidily.

Two videos go up on the very same day. One posts steadily, one blows up. Let us see who wins.
The steady channel adds the same three views every single day. That draws a straight line: f of x equals three x plus four.
The viral video doubles every day instead. That draws a curve that bends upward: y equals two to the x.
Early on, the steady line is actually ahead. Slow and steady leads in the first few days.
But the curve is catching up fast. On day four they meet — both sitting at sixteen views.
After that, the viral curve rockets past and never looks back. That is exponential growth.
Now let us find the steady channel exactly. How many views does it have on day five? We evaluate f of five.
Evaluate means swap every x for the day number. So x becomes five: three times five, plus four.
First the multiplying part. Three times five is fifteen.
Then add the four views it started with. Fifteen plus four is nineteen.
So on day five the steady channel has nineteen views. That is the number to tap: nineteen.
One more, a different kind of question. A new video posts, and its rule is y equals two to the x. We have to say which family it belongs to.
Steady posting means the views go up by the SAME amount every day. Plus three, plus three, plus three. Equal jumps make a straight line.
Going viral means the views MULTIPLY every day instead. Times two, times two, times two. That bends upward.
So read this rule day by day. Day one gives two views. Day two gives four. Day three gives eight. Day four gives sixteen.
Now look at the jumps between them. Two to four is a jump of two. Four to eight is a jump of four. Eight to sixteen is a jump of eight.
The jumps are not equal — they keep growing. So this is not adding the same amount each day. It is multiplying by two each day.
That makes it a curve, not a line. So drop it into going viral.

Here is the plan. A round zone is sized by its area — pi times the radius squared — and we keep pi as pi, so the answer stays a tidy whole number. Then we move props around the level: sliding them, mirroring them across a line, spinning them about the centre. Let us work one of each, nice and slow.
Welcome to the level editor. Let's drop a round zone onto the map. Its radius is three — that's from the middle out to the edge.
To fit this zone into the level we need its area — how much ground it covers.
The rule for the area of any circle is pi times the radius squared.
So we start with the radius. Here it is — three squares from the centre to the edge.
Now square the radius. Squaring three means three rows of three little squares.
Count them up — three rows of three is nine. So r squared is nine.
Now the pi. We are not going to multiply it out into a long decimal — we keep pi as pi.
Nine of them. The area is nine pi.
So the number that goes in front of pi is nine. That is the one you would tap.
Now a different job. This prop sits at three across, two up — and we need its mirror image.
The gold dashed line is the mirror. Here it is the x-axis, running straight across the level.
A mirror image sits the same distance from the mirror, straight opposite. The prop is two squares above the line.
So drag it straight down. One square — it is now one above the line.
Two squares — it is sitting right on the mirror. Not there yet; the mirror is the halfway mark, not the finish.
Keep going, the same distance again. Three squares — one below the line.
Four squares — two below. Now it is two below the mirror, matching the two above. That is the reflection.
Look at the small ring on the travel line: the halfway point sits exactly on the mirror. That is what tells you a reflection is right.
And read the coordinates. The three across never changed — only the up-down flipped, from two to negative two.
A round zone with radius 5. The distance around it is two pi r. How many pi is that?
Circumference = 2 π r. Double the radius: 2 × 5 = 10. So the edge is 10 π.
Mirror the prop at negative 3, 2 across the x axis. Drag it to where the reflection sits.
The x-axis is the mirror, so x stays −3 and y flips to the other side: 2 becomes −2. It lands on (−3, −2).
A cone tower with radius 4 and height 6. A cone holds one third of the silo that would fit around it. How many pi is that?
A cone is a third of the cylinder around it. That cylinder is π r² h = 16 × 6 = 96 π. A third of 96 is 32, so the cone is 32 π.
It was 32π.
Slide the prop at negative 1, 2 by negative 2 across and negative 1 up. Drag it to where it lands.
Sliding adds to each coordinate: x goes −1 −2 = −3, y goes 2 −1 = 1. It lands on (−3, 1).
It was (−3, 1).
A silo with radius 4 and height 3. Its volume is pi r squared, times the height. How many pi is that?
Volume = π r² h. Square the radius: 4² = 16. Then × 3: 16 × 3 = 48. So the volume is 48 π.
It was 48π.

Good news — you already have three dollars saved. That is your head start, sitting at the bottom of the jar.
And every week you drop in five dollars more. So your savings grow five dollars at a time.
After x weeks, the weekly saving adds up to five x, and you still have that three dollars on top.
You can afford it when your savings reach twenty-eight dollars. So five x plus three equals twenty-eight — that is the equation.
To find x, get it on its own. First undo the plus three — take the three-dollar head start off both sides.
Twenty-eight minus three is twenty-five. So five x equals twenty-five — that part comes purely from weekly saving.
Now undo the times five. Split that twenty-five into equal five-dollar weeks.
Watch the jar fill one week at a time — five, ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five.
That took five weeks. So x equals five.
Add back your three-dollar head start and the jar hits twenty-eight — skateboard unlocked. Five weeks!
One more, a harder kind. The jar has twenty-eight dollars in it — but this time money is going OUT.

Every week you spend four dollars. So after x weeks the jar holds twenty-eight minus four x, and that has to stay at or above eight.
Take the bus money off both sides. Negative four x is at least negative twenty.
Now divide both sides by negative four. Here is the part to watch: dividing by a NEGATIVE flips the direction. At least becomes at most.
So the boundary week is five. Set the dot on five.
Check it against the jar. Five weeks of spending four dollars is twenty dollars, and the jar lands exactly on the eight-dollar bus line.
Fewer weeks leaves more in the jar, so those are fine. More weeks eats the bus money. Shade five and everything below it.

Here's a section of the wall. Two holds: the second one sits three across and four up from the first.
Across and up meet at a square corner, so the straight gap between the holds is the long side of a right triangle.
The Pythagorean theorem ties them together: the two sides squared add up to the gap squared.
Start with the three across. Square it — build a three-by-three square out from that side.
A three-by-three square holds nine little squares. So three squared is nine.
Now the four up. Square that one too — a four-by-four square out from that side.
A four-by-four square holds sixteen. So four squared is sixteen.
Now add the two squares together: nine plus sixteen.
Nine plus sixteen is twenty-five. So the gap squared is twenty-five.
To undo the square and get the gap itself, take the square root of both sides.
The square root of twenty-five is five. Watch the gap draw in as its length counts up.
So those two holds are five apart. Five is the number you would tap.
Same wall, a whole route this time. The top hold is six across and six up, and the straight climb to it is root seventy-two.
Root seventy-two is an awkward number. But the climb is made of moves — so find one move you can repeat the whole way.
Try the smallest one: one across, one up. Its own gap is one squared plus one squared, which is two — so that move is root two long.
Lay the first one down. One move of root two.
And another, the exact same shape. Two moves.
Three. Notice the number in front is just how many moves you have made.
Four. Five.
Six — and that lands right on the top hold. Six moves of root two.
So root seventy-two IS six root two. Same climb, counted two ways: one long line, or six equal moves. Check it — six squared is thirty-six, times two is seventy-two.
And that is why like moves add. Two root two plus three root two is just two moves plus three moves — five moves, five root two. Different shapes could never be counted together.

Here is the plan. Your leaderboard score can go above zero when you win and below zero when you lose. To find the new score we combine the swings — adding, subtracting, or multiplying signed numbers — and set the meter. Let us work one out together, nice and slow.
Here's the leaderboard. This round you won three points, then you lost five. Let's find your new score.
On the score meter, a win pushes you UP, above the zero line. A loss pushes you DOWN, below it.
So this round is plus three, then minus five. Put together, that is three minus five.
Start with the win. Plus three lifts the marker to three notches above the zero line.
Now spend the loss of five, one notch at a time. Down one — to two.
Down two — to one.
Down three — and the marker lands right on the zero line. Level.
Still two more to drop. Down four — the marker slips below the line, into the red, to negative one.
Down five — the final notch. It settles on negative two.
Count it up: five notches down from three lands on negative two — below the line.
That is your new score: negative two. Set the meter to negative two.
Now a harder one. Three penalty cards were handed out — and the referee is about to look at them again.
Each penalty card is worth negative four. That is the second number: what one card IS.
There are three of them. Lay out the second.
And the third. Three penalty cards, worth negative four each.
Now the first number, negative three. The minus sign is not part of the count — it is the ACTION. Minus means revoke them.
So revoke all three. Watch the score: taking away a penalty pushes it UP, not down.
That is why negative three times negative four is positive twelve. Take away a penalty enough times and your score climbs.

Here is the plan. Followers growing steadily over weeks form a straight line, written y equals m x plus b. The b is where they start — the intercept. The m is how many they gain each week — the slope. To build the line, we set the start and the growth. Let us do one together, nice and slow.
Here's a creator, and this is their followers over the weeks. We're going to build the growth line — where it starts, and how fast it climbs.
Across the bottom we count the weeks. Going up, we count the followers. Every point says: at this week, this many followers.
In week zero they started with one follower. That first spot is the y-intercept — we call it b. So b is one.
Now, how fast do they grow? Step across just one week. That sideways move is the run, and the run is one.
Over that one week they gained two followers, so we climb up two. That upward move is the rise, and the rise is two.
There's one full step of the staircase: right one week, up two followers.
The slope, m, is the rise divided by the run — two divided by one, which is two. That is two new followers every week.
And it keeps going — another week, up two again; another week, up two again. The same climb, every single week.
Join all those steps together and they line up into one straight line — the growth line. Watch the followers climb from one up to five.
We read it as y equals m x plus b. The m is two, the b is one — so y equals two x plus one.
Start at one, grow by two each week: y equals two x plus one.
One more — this time on the dials you will actually use. This creator starts with two followers and gains one a week.
There are two dials under the grid. START is where week zero sits — that is the b. GROWTH PER WEEK is how fast it climbs — that is the m.
Set START to two. Watch the dot lift to two followers, where the line begins.
Now GROWTH PER WEEK. One follower a week, so nudge it up to one — and the line tips into a climb.
That is the line: y equals x plus two. When yours looks like this, press PLOT THE GROWTH. Now it is your turn.

You're at the phone shop comparing two plans. Each plan's cost is a line — dollars going up, gigabytes going across.
Plan A is pay as you go: one dollar a month, plus two dollars every gigabyte. Cheap to start, but it climbs steeply.
Plan B charges three dollars a month, but only one dollar a gigabyte. It starts higher and climbs gently.
Scan across to one gigabyte. Plan A is three dollars, Plan B is four. Plan A is the cheaper deal here.
Now scan to three gigabytes. Plan A has climbed to seven dollars, Plan B is only six. They have swapped over.
So somewhere in between, the two dots meet. At that usage both plans cost exactly the same.
That meeting spot is the break-even point — where the two lines cross. Watch it light up.
To find it exactly, set the two costs equal: two x plus one equals x plus three.
Take one x away from both sides. That leaves x plus one equals three.
Now take the one dollar fee off both sides, so x is on its own.
x is two. Two gigabytes. If a question ever asks only how many gigabytes until the plans tie, that number is the answer.
Put two back into either plan: two times two plus one is five dollars. The marker rises to the crossing.
There it is — the plans break even at two gigabytes, five dollars. Move the marker onto that crossing.

Two receipts from the same shop, and nobody wrote down what one of anything costs.
The first says three of A and two of B came to sixteen pounds. On its own that is hopeless — loads of price pairs would do it.
The second says one of A and four of B came to twenty two. Also hopeless on its own. But the same two prices have to explain both.
So make one of the items cancel. Multiply the whole second receipt by three: three of A and twelve of B, sixty six pounds.
Both now have three of A. Take the first away from it and the A vanishes completely: ten of B is fifty pounds.
So B is five pounds.
Now put that back into either receipt. Three of A plus two fives is sixteen, so three of A is six, and A is two pounds.
Two pounds and five pounds. Check it against the second receipt: two, plus four fives, is twenty two. Both agree.
Now the shopping as a table. Top row is what one person bought, bottom row the other; the columns are items A and B.
Here is a second week in the same shape. To combine them you add the cells that match — never across.
Top left: two A last week, one A this week. Three.
Top right: one B and five B. Six.
Bottom left: three and two. Five.
Bottom right: four and two. Six.
And that is the whole thing. A table keeps each item in its own column, so adding two weeks never mixes the A count up with the B count.

The faint curve is one year of daylight — how many hours the sun is up, from January round to January.

A big wheel is a circle with a pod on it, and everything in this chapter is just a way of saying where that pod has got to.
Its position is written across first, then up — both measured from the middle of the wheel, not the ground.
This pod is at a half across and root three over two up. Root three over two is about nought point eight seven, so it is much higher than it is far across.
Both numbers are positive, so it is still in the first quarter — up and to the right.
And it is well past halfway up that quarter, because up is so much bigger than across. Keep riding.
There. Sixty degrees. Across a half, up root three over two — which is exactly where we were told the pod was.
Now the third quarter of the ride — round the far side and heading back down.
Across is measured from the middle of the wheel, so anything left of the middle counts as negative.
In the third quarter the pod is on the left, so across is negative.
Up works the same way from the middle: below it counts as negative. In the third quarter the pod is below the centre.
So in the third quarter both are negative. You never have to remember that — you just have to know which side of the middle the pod is on.

At 270° the pod is at (0, −1) — across first, up second.
Cosine is the first of those, so it is 0.
What is the reference angle of 135 degrees?
135° is in quarter 2 of the ride.

Point a torch straight at a wall and the light lands as a circle. That circle is a slice through the cone of light.
Every other shape in this chapter is the same cone, sliced at a different angle. Nothing else changes.
Here is the equation. Two squared terms, added together — so the light closes into a loop rather than opening out.
But they are divided by different numbers, nine and four. That means one direction is stretched more than the other.
A stretched loop is an ellipse, and you get one by tilting the torch part-way. Watch the patch pull out sideways.
Keep going and at sixty degrees one edge of the beam runs parallel to the wall — the light stops closing and you get a parabola.
Past that it opens right out into a hyperbola. Added is a loop, subtracted is a hyperbola, and one square on its own is a parabola.
This one was added and stretched, so it is an ellipse. Back to the tilt that makes one.
Now stand square on again, so the patch is a circle, and ask where on the wall it actually landed.
A squared thing is never negative, so each of these two parts is smallest when it is zero.
The first one is zero when x minus two is zero — so two across.
The second is zero when y plus three is zero. Plus three, so that is negative three up. The sign inside always flips on the way out.
So the middle of the patch is two across, three down. The sixteen on the right has nothing to do with where it is — that is how big it is.
What is the radius of this circle?
The right-hand side is r², so r² = 4.
The number that gives 4 when multiplied by itself is 2.
Which conic section is x squared plus y squared equals twenty five?
Both squares are added and they are scaled the same, so nothing is stretched — that is a circle, and the torch is square on.
So hold the torch square on to the wall.
It was circle.
What is the vertex of this parabola?
The bracket empties at x = −3 — the number inside, with its sign flipped.
At that point nothing is added, so the height is just the −4 outside.
The tip is (−3, −4).
The right-hand side is r², so r² = 25.
The number that gives 25 when multiplied by itself is 5.
The right-hand side is r², so r² = 36.
The number that gives 36 when multiplied by itself is 6.
An ellipse is x squared over 16 plus y squared over 4 equals one. How far does it reach along its long direction?
The bigger denominator is 16, and it sits under x² — so that is the long direction.
That number is the reach squared, so the reach is 4.
The right-hand side is r², so r² = 16.
The number that gives 16 when multiplied by itself is 4.
At that point nothing is added, so the height is just the 1 outside.

A squared part is zero only when the thing inside it is zero.
The x part vanishes at 4 and the y part vanishes at −2.
So the centre is (4, −2) — the number inside comes out with its sign flipped.
The right-hand side is r², so r² = 9.
The number that gives 9 when multiplied by itself is 3.

You bought a phone on credit. Two things are now happening to it every month, and they go in opposite directions.
The base is the whole story. It is simply what one month does to the number.
This base is a half. Multiply by a half and you are left with half of what you had.
Half is left, so half is gone. As a change, that is minus fifty percent every month.
Set the dial that way and the bars fall — the handset losing its resale value, month after month. That is decay.
A base above one would leave you with MORE than you had, and the bars would climb instead. That is the debt.
Now the debt. You owe fifty pounds and it doubles every month you leave it alone.
The dashed line is four hundred pounds. The question is not how much — it is WHEN.
Start by taking the fifty you owed out of it. Four hundred divided by fifty is eight.
So the real question is how many doublings make eight. Two, four, eight — three of them.
And that is a log: log base two of eight is three. The log did not ask how much, it asked how long.
Slide the marker to month three and it lands exactly where the curve meets the line.

Here is a colder week, written as two brackets multiplied together.
Freezing is the dashed line. We want the days the temperature is exactly on it.
A multiplication only comes out as zero when one of the things being multiplied is itself zero. So take the brackets one at a time.
x minus two is zero on day two. So day two is a crossing.
And x minus five is zero on day five. That is the second one.
Two brackets, two crossings — and between them is the stretch of the week that actually stayed below freezing.
The forecaster has fitted a curve to a week of temperature. Ask it what happens outside that week and it will happily answer.
Only the biggest term matters out there. Far from the week, everything else is a rounding error next to x cubed.
Three is odd, and an odd power keeps the sign of whatever you put in. So the two ends do opposite things — they split.
Now the minus in front. Put in a big positive day and x cubed is big and positive, and the minus turns it upside down.

A listing has four reviews in: five, five, four, five. That is nineteen stars between them, and an average of four point seven five.
A fifth review is being written right now. Whatever it says, the printed average is about to be shared out across five instead of four.
Say we want to know which rating would drag that average all the way down to four point zero.
Work backwards. Five reviews averaging four means the five of them add up to twenty.
Nineteen of those twenty are already there. So the one still to come has to be a single star.
And look what that one review did. Four happy customers, one furious one, and the number everybody reads has fallen three quarters of a star.
Line them up in order, though, and the middle review is still a five. That is the difference between a mean and a median: one gets dragged, the other barely notices.

This is the curves panel in a photo editor, and it is a function drawn out: the setting you feed in, and the adjustment that comes out.
The faint dotted curve is the filter we started with. We want the new one, g of x equals f of x minus two.
The minus two is inside the bracket, so it changes the input, not the output. Almost everyone shifts it left the first time.
But watch. Feed in a setting of two. Inside the bracket that becomes two minus two, which is zero — so g at two does what f used to do at zero.
The filter now needs a setting two HIGHER to do the same thing it used to. That is a shift to the RIGHT, not the left.
So a change inside the bracket always moves the curve the opposite way to its sign. Outside the bracket is the one that behaves — plus lifts it, minus drops it.

Your running app shows two different numbers, and it is worth knowing why. One is your average pace for the run. The other is the pace right now.
Average pace is easy, because it needs two moments. Take minute three, and minute five — two minutes apart.
Over that window the average pace works out at eight.
Now shrink the window. Minute three to minute four and a half — and the average drops to seven.
Shrink it again, and it is six and a half.
And again. Six and a quarter.
Watch what those numbers are doing. Eight, seven, six and a half, six and a quarter — every time the window halves, they close in on six.
They never actually reach it, because a window of zero has nothing to average. But six is clearly where they are heading, and that is the pace at that single instant. That is the derivative.
